pageCache.pageTitle: Spiritual, Moral, Social, Cultural (SMSC) – Hall Mead School
pageCache.text:
There is more to school than learning and exams in each subject.
Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural development is the term used to embrace this broader dimension. It ranges from teaching in RE, PSHEE and Citizenship through to assemblies, charity work, cultural awareness days and a wide range of extra curricular and out of school activities. All subjects provide opportunities to promote pupils’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural development. A significant contribution is also made by the school ethos, effective relationships throughout the school, collective worship, and other activities.
Spiritual development
Pupils’ spiritual development involves the growth of their sense of self, their unique potential, their understanding of their strengths and weaknesses, and their will to achieve. As their curiosity about themselves and their place in the world increases, they try to answer for themselves some of life’s fundamental questions. They develop the knowledge skills, understanding, qualities and attitudes they need to foster their own inner lives and non-material wellbeing.
Moral development
Pupils’ moral development involves pupils acquiring an understanding of the difference between right and wrong and of moral conflict, a concern for others and the will to do what is right. They are able and willing to reflect on the consequences of their actions and learn how to forgive themselves and others. They develop the knowledge, skills and understanding, qualities and attitudes they need in order to make responsible moral decisions and act on them.
Social development
Pupils’ social development involves pupils acquiring an understanding of the responsibilities and rights of being members of families and communities (local, national and global), and an ability to relate to others and to work with others for the common good. They display a sense of belonging and an increasing willingness to participate. They develop the knowledge, skills, understanding, qualities and attitudes they need to make an active contribution to the democratic process in each of their communities.
Cultural development
Pupils’ cultural development involves pupils acquiring an understanding of cultural traditions and an ability to appreciate and respond to a variety of aesthetic experiences. They acquire a respect for their own culture and that of others, an interest in others’ ways of doing things and curiosity about differences. They develop the knowledge, skills, understanding, qualities and attitudes they need to understand, appreciate and contribute to culture.

SEND at Hall Mead School
At Hall Mead School, we aim to provide every pupil with the opportunity to succeed and achieve high standards. Our values of beating your best, burning brighter, being kind, and valuing difference guide our approach and expectations for all students, regardless of their starting point or learning barriers.
We consider pupils’ diverse abilities, backgrounds, experiences, interests, and strengths when planning our teaching and learning approaches. We recognise that difficulties can be subject and/or context specific, and we work to target support where it is needed.
Engagement with carers and parents is essential to understanding and supporting each child. Our focus is on developing independence and minimising reliance on support, believing that the right amount of challenge helps students with additional needs grow.
Over 40% of students may need additional support during their school life, but many barriers are temporary and can be managed or overcome with timely, targeted support. Support varies based on the nature of the barriers and is provided through a graduated approach, supplementing the school’s pastoral offer.
Identification of SEND
Where a pupil is identified as having SEND, the SENDCO or Assistant SENDCO will communicate with the parents and pupil to ensure that appropriate educational provisions are in place. Active participation from both pupils and parents is encouraged in discussions regarding the pupil’s needs and support. The SEND department gathers relevant information to identify individual needs and implement suitable support strategies. Parents are engaged in the process to complete individual Pupil Profiles.
For students with an Education, Health, and Care Plan (EHCP), annual reviews are conducted. Input from students, parents, school, and relevant agencies (when applicable) is incorporated to formulate an action plan.
Levels of support
A diagnosis of a particular condition does not necessarily mean that support is required. Most students can access lessons without support when their needs are considered by staff and Quality First Teaching is delivered.
For students who do access the mainstream curriculum but have additional targeted support this takes place in the school’s Nurture Base. Here lessons range from literacy, numeracy and social skills to language development and more bespoke approaches to emotional regulation. Where possible withdrawal from lessons is minimised and targeted work lasts only as long as necessary. Hall Mead School is an Outstanding school, it is important that students are included in lessons as much as possible.
Students who require an ongoing high level of support including an adapted curriculum and/or have specific environmental needs are taught in the school’s Specialist Base. Here students spend over 50% of their time in small group lessons and the adapted curriculum mirrors that of the mainstream school.For more information, please read the school’s SEND Information Report and the Trust SEND policy. If you have concerns or questions about your child, please complete the SEND referral form.
Transition and Preparation for Adulthood
During transition periods, discussions will take place to ensure that appropriate support is provided. For pupils with EHCPs the SENCO is invited to Year 6 annual reviews to assist with transition arrangements. The Year 9 annual review will consider the same areas as other reviews but will focus on options and preparing for adulthood.
In Year 11, discussions about post-16 courses and applications will occur, ensuring that students and parents receive support during this transition. The SENCO will forward relevant information to the next placement and provide additional details upon request.
Exam Access Arrangements
Exam Access Arrangements allow pupils with specific needs, such as special educational needs, disabilities, or temporary injuries, to participate in assessments without altering the assessment’s demands. These arrangements must reflect the pupil’s normal way of working, be considered on a subject-by-subject basis, and must not unfairly advantage or disadvantage the pupil.
Pupils eligible for access arrangements include those with cognition and learning needs, communication and interaction needs, sensory and physical needs, and social, emotional, and mental health needs. A qualified assessor must assess a pupil’s eligibility for Access Arrangements; these assessments take place from the Summer Term of Year 9. Parents will be informed if an assessment is required.
Various types of access arrangements are available, such as supervised rest breaks, extra time, use of a reader or computer reader, scribe or speech recognition technology, and use of a word processor. Chapman House gets its name from the first head boy at the school. The pupils voted for the head boy and Kevin Chapman was elected each year that he was in the school so not only was he the first head boy, but was also head boy for seven years! Chapman House is identified by the colour blue.
Dickens House gets its name from the first Headteacher of Hall Mead School when it opened in 1960 as a secondary modern school. Dickens House is identified by the colour green.
Talbot House gets its name from a now extinct breed of hunting dog that was used in the hunting grounds where the school now stands. Talbot House is identified by the colour red.
Waltham House gets its name from the land which the school is built on which used to be the hunting grounds for Waltham Abbey. Waltham House is identified by the colour gold.

Behaviour and Responses
At Hall Mead, we work hard to maintain clear and positive communication with parents and carers. We use the Headteacher’s Newsletter and Edulink to share information and highlight upcoming events, alongside individual emails and phone calls where necessary.
The best way to ensure students’ progress and wellbeing is for school, home, and students themselves to work together towards shared aims. Young people can sometimes present different versions of events – or only part of the story – when seeking support from home. When school and parents communicate openly and work together, we are best able to support students in making positive choices.
Many of you chose Hall Mead after months, sometimes years, of research, visits, and conversations with others. We value that trust and take our responsibility for your child’s education very seriously.
Educating young people is about far more than academic outcomes. Schools have a statutory responsibility to help develop good citizens and to support students’ Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural (SMSC) development.
During our induction events we explain clearly that children will sometimes make mistakes. Being impulsive, making poor choices or not thinking through the consequences of actions are natural parts of adolescence. You will see this outside school just as we see it within school.
However, recognising that mistakes happen does not mean that they do not require a response.
A response refers to any action or intervention the school puts in place following undesirable behaviour, a breach of our values, or breaking school rules. Responses may be informal or formal, immediate, or planned. They may be educational, reflective, restorative or, where necessary, punitive.

Arcadia, meaning a place offering peace and simplicity, is a club set up to combat mental health issues. Fortnightly, students meet to relax in a stress-free environment. Students can detox from any worries inside or outside of school. Promoted by our student wellbeing ambassadors, the club aims to create a positive atmosphere for students inside of school.
